views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Publish the already-scheduled June 15 Section 301 list and implement the 25% duties on the ~$50B of Chinese industrial and tech goods tied to forced technology transfer and Made in China 2025. Do not add a new $100B tranche and do not unwind the list for another vague purchase pledge. Keep a negotiating channel open for verifiable IP, licensing, and investment-rule changes, and treat any further ZTE relief as contingent on those structural items rather than as a standalone concession.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is a mild US opportunity, not a crisis. The USTR 301 record (2018-03-22) found Chinese joint-venture, licensing, acquisition, and cyber practices impose at least $50B a year of harm, and the November 2017 Beijing commercial package produced no structural IP concessions. The May 19 joint statement only promised that China would “significantly increase” purchases; Mnuchin called the war “on hold,” then the White House on May 29 put the $50B/25% action and June 30 investment restrictions back on because that framework did not fix the 301 findings. US macro is still strong—Michigan sentiment 98.2, industrial production rising, VIX ~13 on 2018-06-13—so the dispute is not yet a material GDP shock. Bilateral goods remain lopsided (June IMPCH ~$44.5B vs EXPCH ~$10.9B), which is the leverage the 301 list is designed to use. The offsetting risk is real but contained: China has already answered $3B on steel/aluminum (2018-04-02) and proposed a matching ~$50B list aimed at soybeans, autos, and aircraft (2018-04-04); Chinese buyers have paused US soybean purchases (~$14B, ~60% of US soy exports) and farm-state political pressure is up. That is sectoral pain, not an existential supply-chain or ally-cohesion threat, so the reading sits near -0.2 rather than -0.5. Action should therefore be moderate escalation of the teed-up 301 tariffs, not a hold or another purchase-only pause: blinking again after May 29 would teach Beijing that MOUs suffice, while a $100B consumer-goods expansion would raise US costs and invite broader retaliation before structural talks have been tested against a live, bounded tariff. The June 7 ZTE $1B-fine/monitor deal already spent a major non-tariff chip and drew a bipartisan Senate NDAA amendment (2018-06-11/12); further non-tariff giveaways without IP deliverables would spend remaining leverage and split the domestic coalition that still backs toughness on China.
key_factors: Section 301 finding of >=$50B annual IP/tech-transfer harm and a June 15 list already teed up after the May 29 truce collapse
May 19 joint statement offered only purchase volume, repeating the Nov 2017 pattern of commercial MOUs without structural IP concessions
US real economy still healthy (sentiment, IP, low VIX); tariffs not yet in force, so threat is leverage plus farm-sector exposure rather than recession
China matching $50B list and soybean-order freeze hit a politically sensitive US export, arguing against a $100B broadening
ZTE denial-order relief already granted; Senate rebuke shows further non-tariff concessions without IP deliverables would cost credibility

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory. Trump signs presidential memorandum directing tariffs on Chinese imports, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
China announces proposed retaliatory tariffs on ~$50B of US goods (including soybeans, automobiles, and aircraft) in response to the Section 301 list.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment latest 98.2 (2018-06-01), still elevated; dispute not showing up as a confidence collapse.
US goods imports from China still ~$44.5B in June 2018 vs exports to China ~$10.9B (EXPCH), preserving US goods-market leverage.
VIX 12.94 on 2018-06-13 after a brief 17 spike on the May 29 truce-break, consistent with contained financial stress.
Interagency estimate that China's tech-transfer/IP policies result in harm to the US economy of at least $50 billion per year; proposed 25% duties on aerospace, ICT, and machinery.
May 29: 25% tariff on $50B Chinese tech imports; full list by June 15; investment limits by June 30; MOFCOM said the steps run against the recent Washington consensus.
Chinese buyers canceling US soybean orders ahead of a possible 25% tariff; ~60% of US soybeans typically shipped to China; farm-belt political exposure.
June 7 ZTE deal: additional $1bn fine, board/executive changes, US-chosen compliance monitors in exchange for lifting the denial order; Trump framed it as part of a larger trade deal.
Bipartisan Cotton-Van Hollen-Schumer NDAA amendment to reinstate the ZTE ban and restrict Huawei/ZTE, a rebuke of the administration's relief.
